sources.news_title: New York City votes to end century-old horse-drawn carriage industry
sources.text:
The New York City Council has voted to end the Big Apple’s horse-drawn carriage industry, which has been around for more than 160 years.
The legislation passed in a 40-7 vote on Thursday afternoon. Its approval came just over a week after New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani made a deal with City Council Speaker Julie Menin to ban horse-drawn carriages in less than two years.

sources.news_title: New York City bans horse-drawn carriages from June 2028
sources.text:
By Maria Tsvetkova
NEW YORK, Oct 22 (Reuters) – The New York City Council voted on Thursday to ban horse-drawn carriages from city streets and Central Park beginning in June 2028, ending a historic tourist attraction and long-standing industry.
Out of the city’s 51 lawmakers, 40 supported the bill, which was backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who earlier this month said the horse-drawn carriage industry would come to an end. Seven council members voted against it and two abstained.
Support for the ban grew after the death this summer of Romanch Mahajan, an 18-year-old tourist from India. Mahajan was thrown from a carriage and died on June 17, when the horse bolted after the driver stepped away to take a picture of Mahajan’s family.
President Donald Trump, who has both attacked Mamdani and held cordial meetings with him, expressed skepticism about the ban.
“When there is a car accident in the area, of which there are many, they don’t stop cars from entering the Park. So why would they stop the Carriages? It was a Great Tradition. Another piece of History that’s gone. It will be missed!” Trump, whose business empire is headquartered in Trump Tower, minutes from Central Park, wrote on Truth Social.
The bill requires the city to develop a transition plan for the workforce by April and to consider a program to compensate carriage operators for their businesses and help with the disposition of their horses. Under the proposal, the horses could not be slaughtered.
The day before the vote, the Transport Workers Union, which represents carriage business owners and drivers, said that if the bill is enacted, it will seek a temporary restraining order from a court “the minute the ink dries,” according to a letter sent to New York City Corporation Counsel Steve Banks.
“This may be the first time in City history that a previously licensed profession was banned,” the letter signed by principal attorney Arthur Schwartz said. “The proposed bill deprives the owner of all economically beneficial or productive use of their property.”
(Reporting by Maria Tsvetkova in New York; Editing by Bill Berkrot)

NYC Council passes bill to ban horse carriage rides within 2 years
sources.text:
NYC Council passes bill to ban horse carriage rides within 2 years
The New York City Council passed a bill banning horse-drawn carriage rides in the city by 2028.
Lawmakers voted Thursday afternoon on Romanch's Law. The legislation is named after Romanch Mahajan, 18, who died during a carriage accident in June in Central Park.
The bill is now headed to Mayor Zohran Mamdani to sign.
Supporters of the bill praised the vote and thanked city leaders for advancing the measure.
Betsy Smith, CEO of the Central Park Conservancy, said carriage rides pose a "serious and even fatal safety risk to Park visitors, carriage drivers, and the horse themselves. Our hearts break for the family of Romanch Mahajan, who stepped into a carriage earlier this summer and never thought he might lose his life."
Kathleen Schatzmann, strategic legislative affairs manager at the Animal Legal Defense Fund, called the vote "the start of a more humane and safe approach to New York tourism" and said the law would responsibly phase out the horse-drawn carriage industry while providing support for workers and protections for horses.
The law is making history, as the carriages have been part of the park since its inception more than 160 years ago. It's ending operations in June 2028, with a transition plan for workers and owners required in 2027.
Carriage owners and their families are arguing that the plan doesn't go far enough. They rallied outside City Hall Wednesday and Thursday to push back.
One family said they have spent nearly a century building their business.
"I invested $400,000 two years ago to expand my father's dream, and you're coming here to steal it," said owner Francesco Riccobono.
"We are asking for fairness. We are asking for compassion. We are asking for a seat at the table," said his wife, Natalie.
The Transport Workers Union says it is prepared to challenge the ban in federal court if it passes.
TWU lawyer Ben Kallos said he believes a judge will overturn the legislation.
"They were supposed to figure out what the economic impact was. It's required by the city charter, and if you pull the economic impact analysis, it's blank," he said.
City Council Speaker Julie Menin said in an interview with NY1 that the ban is necessary to protect animals and public safety.
"Forty-two million people use Central Park each and every year, and the horse carriages are operating in a very crowded area. We've had numerous accidents that have happened where horses have been spooked; they've broken free," she said.
Menin said it has been a long-time issue.
"The first city council bill to ban the horse carriage industry happened 19 years ago. So certainly from an animal welfare perspective, this is very important to do," she said.
The bill also calls for humane placement of animals and assistance for displaced workers.
"With a majority of the Council behind us, we have a historic opportunity to protect New Yorkers, visitors, workers, and animals, and we intend to finish the job," said Council Member Christopher Marte.

Summary
New York City's horse-drawn carriage industry, a tourist fixture for more than 165 years, will be phased out by mid-2028 under a bill passed by the City Council. Licenses for carriage horses, horse-drawn cabs, and their drivers stop being issued June 1, 2028, with existing licenses expiring at the end of May 2028. The bill requires "humane disposition" of the horses and a transition plan for more than 150 active drivers by April 2027, including consideration of compensation for owners' businesses, licenses, and equipment. Permits will still be available for parades, weddings, and filming. The decades-long campaign to end the practice gained momentum after the June death of Romanch Mahajan, a teenage tourist from India, in an incident involving a runaway carriage horse. Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal's analysis of public records counted 96 "serious" incidents and 40 horse deaths near Central Park since 1982. The Central Park Conservancy said at a July hearing it does not expect visitation to drop, noting the park draws 42 million visitors a year. The bill goes to Mayor Zohran Mamdani for signature, and Transport Workers Union Local 100 said it intends to challenge it in federal court.

NEW YORK CITY (WABC) -- The New York City Council voted Thursday to ban horse-drawn carriages, a move that will end an industry that has operated in the city since 1858.
The vote for Romanch's Law was 40 to 7 with two exemptions. The bill now heads to the mayor's desk, although it has passed with a veto-proof majority.
"The first bill was introduced into council 19 years ago, that fight ends today," City Council Speaker Julie Menin said ahead of the vote.
Supporters of the legislation argue horse-drawn carriages no longer belong in heavily traveled areas of the city.
"They don't belong in an area that attracts 42 million people a year, pulling a 1,000-pound carriage in record heat," Menin said.
Horse-drawn carriages have long been a draw for tourists in Central Park. Last June, 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who was visiting from India with his family to celebrate his high school graduation, was thrown from a carriage and killed. The proposed legislation would bear his name.
Mahajan's uncle spoke outside City Hall Thursday and vowed that he will never be forgotten.
Supporters of the ban maintain that 80% of New Yorkers want the activity to end.
The city will have to develop a transition plan for drivers, including helping them find jobs over the next two years.
Opposition to the measure has been fierce, with critics calling the bill unconstitutional because it would ban a licensed industry. Christina Hansen of TWU Local 100 said the legislation would harm both people and horses.

"They are taking away from the people that own the carriages, that have medallions like taxi medallions, that they paid 10's 100s of 1000s of dollars for..." Arthur Schwartz of TWU Local 100 said.

The horse-drawn carriages that have cruised through Central Park for more than 150 years will soon be banished from New York City, ending an iconic tradition beloved by tourists but long opposed by animal welfare activists.
For the carriage drivers, it’s unclear what comes next.
“No one can come up with an appropriate answer because there is none,” said Alexus Lawson, a 28-year-old carriage driver from Queens who grew up with horses and has worked as a riding instructor. Now, she worries about what would become of 7-year-old Starlight and her other horses. “Without a job, how can I take care of my horses?”
The New York City Council passed a bill Thursday that would ban horse-drawn carriage rides by June 2028, pulling back the reins after the death of a teenage tourist last spring.
But the one question that has come up time and again — what to do with drivers whose jobs would be eliminated — remains largely unanswered.
The legislation requires Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office to develop a plan by next April to help the more than 150 remaining drivers find other work. That would include career counseling and referrals for openings in the city's transit, hospitality and taxi industries. It also allows the administration to consider some form of compensation for industry workers.
City Hall is working on a detailed plan for the workforce transition and has started discussions on potential compensation, a spokesperson for the mayor said. Mamdani himself has said government has a “civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry.”

Still, the union representing carriage drivers has vowed to file a legal challenge “the minute the ink dries” on the legislation.
Trump opposed the ban, saying a ‘Great Tradition’ will be missed
President Donald Trump, whose namesake Trump Tower is a stone's throw from Central Park, bemoaned the ban and called carriage rides “a quintessential New York experience.”

Two of Mamdani's mayoral predecessors had called to end the industry but neither succeeded.
Former Mayor Bill de Blasio campaigned on ending the rides on day one of his administration but the effort wilted amid a backlash from unions and a big media blitz involving actor Liam Neeson. Eric Adams, the mayor just before Mamdani, floated a ban late in his term but the proposal went nowhere.

The latest push began in June after an 18-year-old Indian tourist, Romanch Mahajan, died after jumping from a runaway carriage during a ride. His death appeared to be the first fatality involving a horse carriage in Central Park since the rides began.
Mahajan's family has personally appealed to the city to end the rides, offering tearful testimony that they thought the rides were safe. His uncle, Gaurav Mahajan, praised the proposal during a rally Thursday, saying “the hour of justice has finally arrived,” as he stood beside local lawmakers and animal welfare activists.
“We're turning our shattering loss into an unbreakable shield of kindness for the city. For months, our family hasn't been allowed to just grieve,” he said. “We've had to fight. We've had to channel our devastating sorrow into a war for change.”
Carriage drivers have expressed sympathy for Mahajan and his family but argue that they are being unfairly targeted because of a single accident.
“It does nothing for alternate employment, for the continuation of our businesses,” said Christina Hansen, a longtime carriage driver and industry spokesperson. “Who’s going to pay my rent while I’m looking for a job?”

sources.news_title: New York bans horse-drawn carriages over safety and abuse concerns
sources.text:
New York bans horse-drawn carriages after 160 years over safety and abuse concerns
After petting a carriage horse in New York's Central Park at the age of five, Alexus Lawson was hooked.
She has driven a carriage in Manhattan's most famous park, pulled by her horses, for six years. But since Lawson heard about the city's vote this week to outlaw the carriages over animal and public-safety concerns, she has been worried.
"What am I supposed to do with my horse?" asked the 28-year-old about her current horse, Starlight. "You're going to tell me I can't work with her anymore? How am I supposed to ensure her health?"
Lawson is one of roughly 200 horse-drawn carriage drivers in Central Park. Use of the carriages has been an at-times controversial tradition for over 160 years that has become a popular tourist activity.
On Thursday, New York City Council voted to pass a ban on the carriages that would start in June 2028. The proposal is backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who said he will help develop a transition plan for workers in the industry.
Several drivers who spoke to the BBC said they did not want new jobs, and disputed claims their horses are mistreated - even as many New Yorkers and tourists welcomed the ban.
"There were a few cases of horses dying in the middle of the park. You can clearly see that they're not taken care of," said New York resident Ron Tsur. "That's not what they're supposed to be doing."
Since 1982, 40 horses working in Central Park have died, according to the Manhattan Borough President's office, which blames issues including overheating and collisions.
New York leaders previously sought a ban, under pressure from animal-rights activists, but faced pushback from city council members and unions representing the workers.
But the ban movement found new momentum this summer.
In June, Romanch Mahajan, a tourist visiting New York with his family from India, was in a carriage when the horse bolted, causing the 18-year-old to fall out and die. The planned ban - named Romanch's Law after the teen - also follows the death this year of a carriage horse, Deniz, who ate a toxic plant in Central Park.
Mahajan's family was at the city council hearing Thursday when lawmakers voted to pass the bill. Council Speaker Julie Menin said the measure would ensure the 18-year-old was "the last soul that we lose to this industry".
'Horses are working animals'
Several Central Park horse carriage drivers who spoke to the BBC said they were devoted to their horses and that the rides did not pose a safety risk.
Lawson, who was nearby on the day Mahajan fell to his death, called the deadly incident "extremely tragic". But she said if the city was really worried about the safety of the horse-drawn carriages, it would outlaw them immediately - not in two years.
The Central Park Conservancy, the non-profit organisation that manages Central Park and supports the carriage ban, said that over the past 13 months alone, there had been seven "horse-related incidents". In May, a driver was taken to the hospital after a spooked horse hit another carriage, causing it to tip over. In January, another horse, named Destiny, ran into traffic near the park, causing a multi-car collision.
Lawson, who owns six horses, pointed out that New York City carriages were the most regulated in the country and said horses enjoyed the stimulation.
"They look at an animal in harness and they see a trap," Lawson said of officials pushing for the ban. "They see a job as something that's terrible. Horses are working animals."
Medet Fidan, a carriage driver for 12 years, feels similarly attached to his horse, calling allegations of mistreatment a joke.
"I spend more time with my horses than my wife and my kids," he said. "They're telling me I'm abusing my horse? No way."
Fidan said he was angry, and that officials were passing a ban without talking in-person to drivers and others in the industry. "If you don't listen to me, how can you come and kill my business, destroy my family's, my livelihood?" he asked.
The city council held a hearing in July, inviting community members, including horse-carriage drivers, to comment.
The legislation to end horse-drawn carriages proposes an "industry transition framework" including potential job placement, training, career counselling, and financial compensation for those in the business.
A spokesperson for Mamdani said his office was involved in planning to find new jobs for these workers - who make around $60,000 (£ 44,000) to $70,000 a year, according to drivers who spoke at the city council hearing.
But the Transport Workers Union, which represents the drivers, said the law does not include guarantees - including compensation - and that the workers would be "economically wiped out".
The union also raised concerns about a lack of funding for individuals and organisations who eventually take in the horses. It argued that thousands end up at slaughter auctions each year.
The bill forbids selling horses for slaughter or for similar work. Carriage owners would be allowed to keep their horses if they choose, said Menin.
'Confining for the horses'
Though carriage drivers say they are committed to the health of their horses, concerns over the animals' well-being were raised in the city for decades.
The carriages have been opposed by animal-rights groups, including one that was founded in response to New York's industry. In 1866, after Henry Bergh witnessed the brutal beating of a carriage horse, he established the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) to protest horses' treatment and other instances of animal abuse.
People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) and a coalition of organisations supporting the horse-carriage ban also oppose the carriages.
Horses can work up to nine hours a day. They are currently restricted to certain entrances of the park, where they stand and wait with drivers to be hired. Customers pay $72.22 for a 20-minute ride, plus $28.89 for every extra ten minutes.
Vanessa Stolle, a German tourist, said she and her family had horses at home - and they do not belong in a noisy park pulling passengers.
"To stand the whole day here – it's loud for them and they can't go to the countryside," she said.
A fellow German tourist, Christian Bauers, disagreed. He remembered seeing the horses when he came to Central Park 20 years ago. "It's part of the culture of New York," he said. "Let them stay. It's cute."
Jeanne Collopy is an animal lover from Colorado, where horses run wild, she said. She worries about accidents in the park that have harmed humans and horses.
"I know there's a union and I hate to have people out of work," she said, adding: "It's a little bit confining for the horses."
Her husband, Chris Koenigs, said the animals were "wonderful" to look at. But the death of the teenager this summer was "sickening", and a high price to pay for enjoying the horses, he said.
"The park is magnificent," he added. "I can't help but think, it would be a magnificent park with or without the carriages."

sources.news_title: NYC Council bans horse carriages in veto-proof vote that will end 150-year-old Central Park tradition
sources.text:
NYC Council bans horse carriages in veto-proof vote that will end 150-year-old Central Park tradition
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Horse-drawn carriages will be banned in New York City after the City Council approved a new bill Thursday that will end a Central Park tradition that’s endured for more than 150 years.
The ban passed in a veto-proof 40-7 vote, with two council members abstaining – despite a last-minute attempt to amend the proposal and push the ban back in 2030.
The ban will take hold on June 1, 2028 and outlaw horse-drawn carriages across all five boroughs.
That means about 200 carriage drivers will see their livelihoods – and entire industry – vanish from the city without a trace in less than two years.
Carriage industry workers quickly returned fire with a pledge to file a lawsuit against the ban, zeroing in on the complete lack of monetary compensation in the bill – which only included vague promises of job training for “new economic opportunities.”
“This bill is a train wreck of constitutional and due process violations,” Transport Workers Union president John Samuelsen said in a statement.
“It offers nothing concrete for blue-collar drivers and carriage owners who will be financially crushed, stripped of their jobs, their licenses, expensive city-issued medallions, small businesses, and way of life,” he added.
“It is not progressive. It is anti-worker. It’s theft.”
The vote ends a years-long saga that has drawn headlines in recent summers due to horses that have collapsed or dropped dead after spending hours working through scorching hot days.
Such incidents have led to fevered discussions about the conditions the carriage horses are made to work in, with critics arguing they’re inhumane.
The controversy came to a head this summer after 18-year-old tourist Romanch Mahajan was killed when a horse carrying his family got spooked and bolted.
Mahajan was thrown from the carriage and died, with his family decrying “the industry responsible” for his death and the ban ultimately being named “Romanch’s Law” after him.
“If [the prior legislation] had passed, the carriages would have stopped on June 1, 2026 — Romanch died on June 17,” his father, Deepak Mahajan, said at a July City Council hearing.
“This was not an unpredictable accident. Let his death not be in vain,” he added.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Council Speaker Julie Menin struck a deal to kill the carriage business earlier in October, citing safety as the primary factor.
But carriage workers – many of whom have said their life-savings are tied up in their operations – have questioned why Mamdani has targeted them when e-bike delivery drivers and pedicab drivers regularly flout traffic laws and cause dangerous accidents.
“Before you became mayor, you participated in a 15-day hunger strike to support yellow taxi medallion owners facing financial ruin,” longtime carriage driver Atakan Aktay said last week. “Now you are mayor, and we face the prospect of losing our businesses without guaranteed compensation.
“Where is that same compassion for us? How can you fight for one group of medallion owners while allowing another group to face financial devastation? To us, that feels hypocritical and humiliating,” Aktay added.
Exactly what will become of the numerous horses involved was not specified in the bill, but is expected to be addressed now that the measure passed.
Animal advocates suggested they could be sent to horse sanctuaries across the country, where they’d be free to live out their lives without being forced into labor.
“New York City is finally ending deadly horse carriage rides,” the outspoken anti-carriage group NYCLASS celebrated in a statement after the bill passed.
“We will work with the administration to ensure the horses retire to safe, loving rescue farms where they can finally run free.

sources.news_title: Facing a ban on horse-drawn carriages, Central Park’s drivers fear for their future
sources.text:
By ANTHONY IZAGUIRRE
NEW YORK (AP) — The horse-drawn carriages that have cruised through Central Park for more than 150 years will soon be banished from New York City, ending an iconic tradition beloved by tourists but long opposed by animal welfare activists.
For the carriage drivers, it’s unclear what comes next.
“No one can come up with an appropriate answer because there is none,” said Alexus Lawson, a 28-year-old carriage driver from Queens who grew up with horses and has worked as a riding instructor. Now, she worries about what would become of 7-year-old Starlight and her other horses. “Without a job, how can I take care of my horses?”
The New York City Council passed a bill Thursday that would ban horse-drawn carriage rides by June 2028, pulling back the reins after the death of a teenage tourist last spring.
But the one question that has come up time and again — what to do with drivers whose jobs would be eliminated — remains largely unanswered.
The legislation requires Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office to develop a plan by next April to help the more than 150 remaining drivers find other work. That would include career counseling and referrals for openings in the city’s transit, hospitality and taxi industries. It also allows the administration to consider some form of compensation for industry workers.
City Hall is working on a detailed plan for the workforce transition and has started discussions on potential compensation, a spokesperson for the mayor said. Mamdani himself has said government has a “civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry.”
Carriage drivers wonder about their future
Medet Fidan, a former cab driver who traded his steering wheel for a set of reins after ride-hailing apps upended the taxi industry, said he felt like he was being targeted.
“I think the city is leaving us a big mess,” said Fidan, 56. “We’re going to lose our businesses, we’re going to lose our jobs, we’re going to lose our livelihoods.”
Council Speaker Julie Menin “will remain engaged in the transition process,” a spokesperson said, adding that the legislation seeks to address the longstanding question of what happens to displaced carriage drivers by setting a firm deadline for City Hall to act.
“These workers deserve to be protected,” Menin said Thursday, adding that horses no longer have a place among Central Park’s pedestrians, cyclists, dog-walkers and gawking tourists.
Still, the union representing carriage drivers has vowed to file a legal challenge “the minute the ink dries” on the legislation.
Trump opposed the ban, saying a ‘Great Tradition’ will be missed
President Donald Trump, whose namesake Trump Tower is a stone’s throw from Central Park, bemoaned the ban and called carriage rides “a quintessential New York experience.”
“It was a Great Tradition. Another piece of History that’s gone. It will be missed!” Trump wrote on social media.
Two of Mamdani’s mayoral predecessors had called to end the industry but neither succeeded.
Former Mayor Bill de Blasio campaigned on ending the rides on day one of his administration but the effort wilted amid a backlash from unions and a big media blitz involving actor Liam Neeson. Eric Adams, the mayor just before Mamdani, floated a ban late in his term but the proposal went nowhere.
Latest push to end the rides began after a tourist’s death
The latest push began in June after an 18-year-old Indian tourist, Romanch Mahajan, died after jumping from a runaway carriage during a ride. His death appeared to be the first fatality involving a horse carriage in Central Park since the rides began.
Mahajan’s family has personally appealed to the city to end the rides, offering tearful testimony that they thought the rides were safe. His uncle, Gaurav Mahajan, praised the proposal during a rally Thursday, saying “the hour of justice has finally arrived,” as he stood beside local lawmakers and animal welfare activists.
“We’re turning our shattering loss into an unbreakable shield of kindness for the city. For months, our family hasn’t been allowed to just grieve,” he said. “We’ve had to fight. We’ve had to channel our devastating sorrow into a war for change.”
Carriage drivers have expressed sympathy for Mahajan and his family but argue that they are being unfairly targeted because of a single accident.
“It does nothing for alternate employment, for the continuation of our businesses,” said Christina Hansen, a longtime carriage driver and industry spokesperson. “Who’s going to pay my rent while I’m looking for a job?”

sources.news_title: NYC Votes to Ban Carriage Horses
NYC horse carriages banned after City Council vote
sources.text:
Horse-drawn carriages, a Central Park presence since 19th century, banned in historic City Council vote as union plans suit
The New York City Council voted on Thursday to abolish the horse-drawn-carriage industry, following years of political tumult that pitted unionized labor against animal-rights activism.
The bill passed late in the afternoon with 40 in favor, 7 against and 2 abstentions. It's almost certain to become law, given the support of Mayor Zohran Mamdani, ending an industry that dates to the 1860s in Central Park.
As voting was getting underway in the council chamber, former New Yorker Donald Trump took to his Truth Social outlet to voice opposition, calling the industry "a quintessential New York experience" and the abolition "So sad."
Throughout Thursday, the City Hall grounds took on a Boschian air: top-hatted coachmen (and coachwomen) clad in outfits from a bygone era pleading for their jobs and threatening to sue; animal-rights activists unfurling equine art and begging NYPD cops to be let past the building gates to witness the vote; a woman in a horse costume on the other side of the building explaining to passersby that she thinks the industry is humane.
The law will ban the industry in New York starting on June 1, 2028, under the latest version of the bill, Introduction 943-A.
The Transport Workers Union of America, which represents the 150 or so active drivers who own and/or operate 68 carriages, is planning to sue to overturn what the council passed as contrary to state and local law, according to union spokesman Pete Donohue. That lawsuit will be filed, he said, once the bill becomes law.
Under a deal reached earlier this month by Mamdani and Council Speaker Julie Menin, there will be job training and, potentially, financial compensation for the drivers and owners and provisions for horses. But there are no guarantees, and it's up to the Mamdani administration to study, and decide the extent of, the compensation, if any.
For over 15 years, the controversy over horse-drawn carriage rides, which take place mostly in Central Park and are typically taken by tourists, has loomed over city politics, influencing elections as stakeholders poured money into campaigns, and candidate after candidate vowed to abolish the industry.
Adding to the intrigue are allegations, made by the union, that the push to ban horses is backed by the real estate industry, purportedly to develop the land on Manhattan’s West Side where the carriage horse stables are located.
Yet long-promised bans never materialized.
That was until momentum toward a ban picked up speed earlier this year, when in June an 18-year-old tourist, Romanch Mahajan, was killed in Central Park after being thrown from a carriage after the carriage horse spooked and bolted.
Trump, apparently referring to the death in his post, called it just "one tragic accident."
"When there is a car accident in the area, of which there are many, they don’t stop cars from entering the Park. So why would they stop the Carriages?" he wrote. (Cars have been banned in city parks for almost a decade, a rule inspired, in part, to prevent crashes.)
Despite the bill's passage, the industry is not going away without a fight.
Pro-horse-carriage demonstrators have protested, hoping to persuade officials to change course. The drivers and their supporters rallied on Thursday morning at City Hall.
Animal-rights activists have long bemoaned the horses’ treatment as cruel, which the horse-drawn carriage industry denies.
The legislation requires "the humane disposition of carriage horses" and would "prohibit their sale or transfer for inhumane purposes, such as for slaughter or for use in another horse drawn cab business."
A "horse drawn cab industry transition plan" would need to be drawn up by April 1, 2027, to include a "workforce transition program, consideration of a program to assist carriage horse owners with the disposition of their horses and equipment, and consideration of a program to provide compensation to horse drawn cab owners," according to a council summary.

A 160-year-old New York tradition is headed for extinction
Animal Wellness Action Celebrates NYC Council Vote to Phase Out Horse-Drawn Carriages
sources.text:
Wayne Pacelle applauds Speaker Julie Menin, bill author Christopher Marte, cosponsors, and Council members for advancing landmark legislation to protect horses and improve public safety
NEW YORK — Animal Wellness Action today celebrated the New York City Council’s vote to phase out the city’s horse-drawn carriage industry, marking a major milestone in the decades-long effort to protect horses from the dangers of working in one of the world’s busiest urban environments. The vote was 40 – 7 with two abstentions, and the bill now goes to Mayor Zohran Mamdani for his signature.
The organization applauded Council Speaker Julie Menin for her leadership in bringing the legislation forward, as well as Council Member Christopher Marte, the bill’s author, its cosponsors, and all Council members who supported the measure. The legislation, known as Romanch’s Law, provides for the phaseout of horse-drawn carriages by June 1, 2028, while establishing a transition plan for carriage drivers and other industry workers.
“It’s about damn time,” said Wayne Pacelle, president of Animal Wellness Action and the Center for a Humane Economy. “As a high school student, I came to Central Park on a field trip and was so depressed seeing the overburdened horses and, in a separate enterprise, tigers and jaguars pacing back and forth in the concrete-and-steel Central Park Zoo. Those zoo exhibits shut down decades ago, and now we will see the carriage horses retired and carriage rides rapidly phased out in the heart of the city. Justice delayed but not denied.”
This is a victory that belongs to the entire animal welfare movement, and especially to our friends at NYCLASS.
“We have been proud to stand alongside our friends at NYCLASS on this issue and are grateful for their tenacity, leadership, and unwavering commitment to protecting these horses,” Pacelle said. “This achievement reflects years of dedicated advocacy and the determination of people who refused to give up on a more humane future for New York City.”
The push to end horse-drawn carriages gained renewed urgency following the deaths of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who suffered fatal injuries in a carriage accident in Central Park in June, and Deniz, a 16-year-old carriage horse who died after reportedly consuming poisonous Japanese yew leaves.
Animal Wellness Action and the Center for a Humane Economy have pledged to help identify humane placement options for carriage horses whose owners relinquish them to qualified animal welfare organizations.
“We look forward to working with NYCLASS and other partners to help ensure that these horses have a safe and humane future beyond the carriage trade,” Pacelle said.
